content: The policies and protocols for monitoring fetal well-being in pregnancies with suspected impaired fetal growth vary significantly, involving numerous combinations of different surveillance methods. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of various antenatal fetal surveillance regimens on critical perinatal and maternal outcomes. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of February 29, 2012. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared the effects of different antenatal fetal surveillance regimens. Two authors, R. Grivell and L. Wong, independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. Only one trial, involving 167 women and their babies, met the inclusion criteria. This trial was a pilot study conducted alongside another study, and no separate sample size calculation was performed. The trial compared a twice-weekly fetal surveillance regimen (which included biophysical profile, nonstress tests, umbilical artery Doppler, middle cerebral artery Doppler, and uterine artery Doppler) with a fortnightly surveillance regimen. In both groups, fetal growth was assessed every two weeks. The data were insufficient to evaluate the primary infant outcome, which was a composite measure of perinatal mortality and serious morbidity. However, there were no perinatal deaths reported in the study. Regarding the primary maternal outcome, which was the rate of emergency cesarean sections performed for fetal distress, no significant difference was observed between the two groups (risk ratio [RR] 0.96; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.35 to 2.63). Interestingly, the mean gestational age at birth was four days earlier in the group receiving twice-weekly surveillance compared to the group receiving fortnightly surveillance (mean difference [MD] -4.00 days; 95% CI -7.79 to -0.21 days). Additionally, women in the twice-weekly surveillance group were 25% more likely to undergo induction of labor compared to those in the fortnightly surveillance group (RR 1.25; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.50). The authors concluded that there is limited evidence from randomized controlled trials to guide best practices for fetal surveillance regimens in pregnancies affected by impaired fetal growth. Further research is necessary to assess the effects of currently used fetal surveillance strategies in such cases.
